claim: Drosophila melanogaster larvae measuring approximately 1 mm in length produce ground reaction forces of 1–7 µN during crawling.
source: Crawling in larvae measuring ~1 mm in length involves an intricate pattern of cuticle sequestration and planting, producing GRFs of 1–7 µN.
evidence: The manuscript presents direct measurements of GRFs using WARP microscopy, with quantitative data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Drosophila larvae insert and expand denticulated, feet-like structures into substrates as they move.
source: We show that larvae insert and expand denticulated, feet-like structures into substrates as they move, a process not previously observed in soft-bodied animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic tracking data in Figures 1-2 and force mapping data in Figures 4-6.

claim: Protopodia form dynamic anchors to compensate counteracting forces during larval locomotion.
source: These 'protopodia' form dynamic anchors to compensate counteracting forces.
evidence: The claim is supported by force measurements showing how protopodia exert forces during different phases of locomotion (Figures 5-6).

claim: Individual denticles exert forces in the range of 1.4–47.5 nN with a median of 11.51 nN.
source: The median force exerted by individual denticles was 11.51 nN (1.4–47.5 nN; n = 130 denticles) across a median area of 2.81 µm (1.15–9.13 µm; n = 130 denticles).
evidence: Direct measurements from ERISM imaging of anaesthetized larvae as shown in Figure 3.

claim: During forward waves, the posterior-most row of denticles initiates movement before the anterior-most row.
source: During forward waves (peristaltic contractions travelling in an anterograde direction), the anterior-most row of each denticle started to move after the corresponding posterior-most row (Figure 2b) and completed its movement after the posterior-most row stopped moving (Figure 2c), that is, there was an anteroposterior (AP) latency for both swing initiation (SI) (when movement begins) and for swing termination (ST) (when movement ends).
evidence: Kinematic tracking data presented in Figure 2 showing temporal differences in movement initiation.

claim: The 'rolling' progression pattern of denticle bands is analogous to the 'heel-to-toe' footfalls of limbed animals.
source: Such a 'rolling' progression pattern is analogous to the 'heel-to-toe' footfalls of limbed animals (Federle and Labonte, 2019).
evidence: The comparison is based on observed kinematic patterns and supported by citation to literature on limbed animals.

claim: Swing initiation latencies scale with wave duration for posterior abdominal segments (A7-A4) with R² values ranging from 0.46 to 0.78.
source: For forward waves and posterior segments, the latencies during the SI period are largely determined by wave duration (R2 range: 0.46–0.78, A7-A4) but this is less the case for anterior abdomen and thorax (R2 range: 0.12–0.35, A3-A1 and T3, Figure 2e).
evidence: Statistical analysis of kinematic data presented in Figure 2e.

claim: Swing termination latencies do not strongly correlate with wave duration (R² range: 0.01–0.26).
source: The magnitudes of ST-related latencies are not strongly determined by wave duration (R2 range: 0.01–0.26, Figure 2f).
evidence: Statistical analysis of kinematic data presented in Figure 2f.

claim: Microcavities with Young's moduli in the range of 10–30 kPa were developed for measuring larval forces.
source: First, we developed optical microcavities with mechanical stiffnesses in the range found in hydrogel substrates commonly used for studying Drosophila larval behaviour, that is, Young's modulus (E) of 10–30 kPa (Ahearne et al., 2005; Salerno et al., 2010; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).
evidence: The development is described with reference to characterization by AFM (Figure 3b-c) and citations to literature on typical substrate stiffnesses.

claim: During swing periods, protopodia detach from the substrate with posterior denticle rows moving to meet anterior rows, inverting the cuticle and sequestering the whole protopodia into a travelling pocket.
source: During SwPs, protopodia detached from the substrate, with the posterior row of denticles moving to meet the anterior row of denticles, thereby inverting the cuticle and sequestering the whole protopodia into a travelling pocket (Figure 1c).
evidence: Direct observation from lateral imaging shown in Figure 1c and Video 1.

claim: When protopodia end their swing period, they unfold from the sequestration pocket and protrude into the substrate during the stance period.
source: When protopodia ended their SwP, they unfolded from the sequestration pocket and then protruded into the substrate during the StP.
evidence: Direct observation from lateral imaging shown in Figure 1c.

claim: In backward waves, the heel-toe-like latency is reversed compared to forward waves, with anterior-led latencies in swing initiation and posterior-led latencies in swing termination.
source: In backward waves, the heel-toe-like latency was reversed, with anterior-led latencies observed in SI and posterior-led latencies observed in ST (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Kinematic tracking data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Larvae travel surrounded by a relatively large water droplet that produces upwardly directed force due to surface tension.
source: We also observed that the animals travel surrounded by a relatively large water droplet. During StP, protopodia displaced the substrate, and during SwP, protopodia local to the contraction were completely removed from the substrate while travelling to their new resting position.
evidence: Direct observation from WARP imaging shown in Figure 4a and Video 3.

claim: 0.5–1 s prior to headsweep initiation, the contact area in posterior segments increases, spreading outwards laterally.
source: 0.5–1 s prior to headsweep initiation, the contact area in posterior segments increased, spreading outwards laterally, employing both the protopodia and the naked cuticle along the midline (Figure 4c).
evidence: WARP imaging data showing temporal changes in contact area before headsweeps (Figure 4b-d).

claim: Tripod formation was observed before all forward waves (n = 28 across six animals) and bilateral thoracic activity (n = 3 across two animals).
source: Tripod formation was seen before all observed forward waves (n = 28 across six animals) and bilateral thoracic activity (n = 3 across two animals), but not all tripod contacts resulted in further behaviour (Figure 4g).
evidence: Quantitative behavioral analysis from WARP imaging experiments presented in Figure 4g.

claim: The mean delay between tripod contact and protopodial detachment in A7 is 0.66 s ± 0.21 s.
source: The mean delay was 0.66 s ± 0.21 s (Figure 4h, n = 20 waves across six animals).
evidence: Temporal analysis of WARP imaging data presented in Figure 4h.

claim: The magnitude of force output is positively correlated with protopodial contact area in a quadratic relationship (A6: Adj. R² = 0.77, A4: Adj. R² = 0.92, A2: Adj. R² = 0.79).
source: We found that the magnitude of force output was positively correlated with protopodial contact area in a quadratic relationship (A6: Adj. R2 = 0.77, A4: Adj. R2 = 0.92, A2: Adj. R2 = 0.79)
evidence: Statistical analysis of force and contact area data from WARP measurements shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The maximum contact area during swing termination is significantly greater than during swing initiation for posterior abdominal segments (p≤0.05 for A8/9-A3) but not for the anterior abdominal protopodium (p>0.05 for A2).
source: The maximum contact area during ST was significantly greater than that during SI for the posterior abdomen (p≤0.05 for A8/9-A3) but not for the anterior abdominal protopodium (p>0.05 for A2) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Statistical analysis of contact area data from WARP measurements presented in Figure 5d.

claim: Peak displaced volume during swing initiation scales with wave duration for larger abdominal segments (A6: R² = 0.69; A4: R² = 0.48) but not for smaller anterior segments (A2: R² = 0.24).
source: The peak of the displaced volumes during SI was largely determined by wave duration (R2 range: 0.48–0.69, A7-A4, Figure 5E), again except for the anterior abdomen (A3: R2 = 0.15; A2: R2 = 0.24).
evidence: Statistical analysis of displacement volume data from WARP measurements shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Peak displaced volume during swing termination does not scale with wave duration (R² range: 0.03–0.05, A7-A2).
source: However, the peak of the displaced volumes during ST did not scale with wave duration (R2 range: 0.03–0.05, A7-A2).
evidence: Statistical analysis of displacement volume data from WARP measurements shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The mean contact delay relative to the most posterior part of the protopodium is 0.035 s ± 0.007 s at 6 µm away, increasing to 0.062 s ± 0.021 s in the middle and 0.253 ± 0.115 s at the most anterior part.
source: The mean contact delay relative to the most posterior part of the protopodium was 0.035 s ± 0.007 s at 6 µm away from the most posterior part and increased to 0.062 s ± 0.021 s and 0.253 ± 0.115 s in the middle and at the most anterior part of the protopodium, respectively (Figure 6c).
evidence: Temporal analysis of high-resolution WARP imaging during swing termination shown in Figure 6c.

claim: At medial distance from the midline, the contact delay relative to the midline is 0.045 s ± 0.022 s (left) and 0.057 s ± 0.019 s (right).
source: At a medial distance from the midline, the contact delay relative to the midline was 0.045 s ± 0.022 s (left) and 0.057 s ± 0.019 s (right).
evidence: Temporal analysis of mediolateral expansion during swing termination shown in Figure 6d.

claim: At the distal left and right of the protopodium, contact occurs 0.111 s ± 0.030 s (left) and 0.165 s ± 0.058 s (right) after midline contact.
source: At the distal left and right of the protopodium, contact occurred 0.111 s ± 0.030 s (left) and 0.165 s ± 0.058 s (right) after midline contact (Figure 6d).
evidence: Temporal analysis of mediolateral expansion during swing termination shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Protopodia insert a medial-spike into the substrate through which swing termination-related peak ground reaction forces are conferred before expanding along the anteroposterior and mediolateral axes.
source: This analysis also showed that protopodia insert a medial-spike into the substrate, through which ST related peak GRFs are conferred, before expanding along the AP and ML axes.
evidence: Analysis of spatiotemporal force patterns during swing termination shown in Figure 6.

claim: Denticle bands are situated upon larger articulated foot-like cuticular processes which act as locomotory appendages.
source: Here, we show that denticle bands are situated upon larger articulated foot-like cuticular processes, which act as locomotory appendages.
evidence: Kinematic tracking and force measurements shown in Figures 1-6 demonstrating the functional role of these structures.

claim: Protopodia dynamically change shape during locomotion, allowing sequestration and presentation of denticles.
source: Protopodia dynamically change shape during locomotion, allowing sequestration and presentation of denticles.
evidence: Direct observation from lateral imaging (Figure 1c) and WARP imaging (Figures 4-6).

claim: Protopodia resemble pseudopodia in cells – transient structures covered with actin protrusions used to facilitate movement.
source: Superficially, protopodia resemble the much smaller pseudopodia in cells – transient structures, similarly covered with actin protrusions, used by cells to facilitate movement (Burnette et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison based on structural and functional similarities, supported by citation to cellular biology literature.

claim: Protopodia show similarities to soft prolegs of Manduca sexta caterpillars but are approximately 30 times smaller.
source: The same function and principles of protopodia may underlie 'creeping welts' noted in larger dipteran larvae (Friesen et al., 2015) and show similarities to soft prolegs of Manduca sexta caterpillars but are approximately 30 times smaller (Lin and Trimmer, 2010).
evidence: Comparative analysis supported by citations to literature on other soft-bodied larvae.

claim: Both deployment and removal of denticle bands involve rolling 'heel-toe' like movements, similar to footfalls in limbed animals including terrestrial arthropods.
source: This suggests that both deployment and removal involved rolling 'heal-toe' like movements, similar to footfalls in limbed animals, including terrestrial arthropods (Federle and Labonte, 2019).
evidence: Kinematic analysis showing sequential contact patterns (Figure 2) and comparison to literature on limbed animals.

claim: Swing initiation latencies scaling with wave duration could be mediated by proprioceptor activity in the periphery.
source: SIs scale with SwP, and this could be mediated by proprioceptor activity in the periphery (Vaadia et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference based on observed scaling relationship and citation to literature on proprioception.

claim: The more random nature of swing termination suggests the process is less finely controlled than swing initiation.
source: In contrast, the more random nature of the ST suggests the process is less finely controlled.
evidence: Inference based on lack of correlation between ST latencies and wave duration (Figure 2f).

claim: The random nature of swing termination could be a consequence of fluid inertia within the animal and/or the release of elastic energy from cuticle or relaxation of muscles.
source: This could be a consequence of fluid inertia within the animal and/or the release of elastic energy from cuticle (Sun et al., 2022) or relaxation of muscles (Simon et al., 2010; Ormerod et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations to relevant literature on biomechanics.

claim: ERISM and WARP allow for probe-free measurement of vertical ground reaction forces with high spatial and temporal resolution.
source: Given ERISM and WARP allow for probe-free measurement of vertical GRFs with high spatial and now temporal resolution, it becomes an attractive method for animal-scale mechanobiology.
evidence: Technical description of the methods and their capabilities, demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: WARP microscopy achieves down to 10 ms temporal resolution.
source: Until recently, this technique was limited by its low temporal resolution (~10 s), making it unsuitable for use in recording substrate interaction during fast animal movements, but a very recent further development of ERISM known as wavelength alternating resonance pressure (WARP) microscopy has been demonstrated to achieve down to 10 ms temporal resolution (Meek et al., 2021).
evidence: Technical specification supported by citation to the WARP development paper.

claim: Drosophila larvae are segmentally organised peristaltic crawlers that move by generating waves of muscle contractions.
source: Drosophila larvae are segmentally organised peristaltic crawlers that move by generating waves of muscle contractions (Berrigan and Pepin, 1995; Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge about larval locomotion supported by citations to literature.

claim: Larvae have segmentally repeating bands comprised of six rows of actin trichomes (denticles).
source: Larvae have segmentally repeating bands comprised of six rows of actin trichomes (denticles) (Payre, 2004).
evidence: Anatomical description supported by citation to literature on larval development.

claim: Natural variations in denticle count across animals do not strongly affect locomotor behaviour.
source: Inversion of the cuticle to remove denticles from the substrate may also explain why natural variations in denticle count across animals do not strongly affect locomotor behaviour (Fitzpatrick and Szewczyk, 2005).
evidence: Inference based on observed sequestration mechanism and citation to literature on denticle variation.

claim: The dynamic anchoring during the progression of peristaltic waves serves to counteract horizontal reaction forces resulting from Newton's third law of motion.
source: The dynamic anchoring during the progression of peristaltic waves thus serves to counteract horizontal reaction forces resulting from Newton's third law of motion.
evidence: Inference based on observed force patterns and fundamental physics principles.

claim: A sequence of positioning points of support and anchoring them against the substrate has long been postulated to be a fundamental process in soft-bodied locomotor systems.
source: Such a sequence of positioning points of support and anchoring them against the substrate has long been postulated to be a fundamental process in soft-bodied locomotor systems (Trueman, 1975) and may be central to explaining why soft-bodied animals have evolved segmentally repeating bodies (Budd, 2001).
evidence: Theoretical framework supported by citations to literature on soft-bodied locomotion and evolution.

claim: Immediately before enacting headsweep, larvae redistribute their body mass into naked cuticle between protopodia along the midline, effectively fusing multiple protopodia into a single 'ultra-protopodia'.
source: Immediately before enacting headsweep, larvae redistributed their body mass into naked cuticle in between protopodia along the midline, effectively fusing multiple protopodia into a single 'ultra-protopodia' that extends across multiple posterior segments.
evidence: Direct observation from WARP imaging shown in Figure 4b-d.

claim: The redistribution of body mass before headsweeps occurs hundreds of milliseconds before the start of a headsweep, suggesting it may be part of an active preparatory behaviour.
source: This redistribution occurs hundreds of milliseconds before the start of a headsweep, suggesting that it may be part of an active preparatory behaviour.
evidence: Temporal analysis of WARP imaging data (Figure 4b-d) showing timing of contact area changes.

claim: Similar preparatory behaviours have been observed in caterpillars before cantilevering behaviours, adult flies during fast escape behaviours, and humans during stepping.
source: Similar preparatory behaviours have been observed in caterpillars before cantilevering behaviours (Lin et al., 2011), adult flies during fast escape behaviours (Card and Dickinson, 2008), and humans during stepping (Watanabe and Higuchi, 2022).
evidence: Comparative analysis supported by citations to literature on preparatory behaviors in other organisms.

claim: Two bilateral cuticular protrusions covered in trichomes, labeled as anal papillae, are likely candidates responsible for tripod-shaped substrate interactions.
source: Two bilateral cuticular protrusions covered in trichomes, labelled in previous work as anal papillae (Zanini et al., 2016), are likely candidates responsible for these substrate interactions.
evidence: Anatomical identification based on imaging (Figure 4e) and citation to literature on larval anatomy.

claim: The actions of tripod papillae structures have not previously been described as part of movement in soft-bodied animals.
source: However, the actions of these structures have hitherto not previously been described as a part of movement in soft-bodied animals.
evidence: Statement of novelty based on literature review.

claim: The tripod processes are ideally positioned to provide an anchor against horizontal reaction force generated by the initial contraction when moving forward.
source: The tripod processes are ideally positioned to provide an anchor against horizontal reaction force generated by the initial contraction when moving forward (Figure 7a) and might effectively form a temporary extra segment prior to initiation of a wave (Figure 7b).
evidence: Inference based on observed timing and position of tripod deployment (Figure 4) and biomechanical modeling (Figure 7).

claim: Larvae do not simply pull protopodia off the substrate in a vertical direction; instead, they horizontally slide posterior regions forward in the axis of travel before invaginating and sequestering friction-generating features.
source: Larvae do not simply pull protopodia off the substrate in a vertical direction; instead, they horizontally slide posterior regions forward in the axis of travel, before invaginating and therefore sequestering friction-generating features (e.g. denticles).
evidence: Direct observation from lateral imaging (Figure 1c) and WARP imaging (Figure 4a).

claim: The sequestration process shows similarities to the use of shearing forces to detach adhesive pads in limbed arthropods.
source: This shows similarities to the use of shearing forces to detach adhesive pads in limbed arthropods (Federle and Labonte, 2019).
evidence: Comparative analysis supported by citation to literature on arthropod adhesion.

claim: The posterior medial region of the protopodia makes a large contribution to peak ground reaction forces exerted during swing termination, similar to a vertebrate heel strike.
source: Specifically, the posterior medial region of the protopodia makes a large contribution to peak GRFs exerted during ST (Figure 7b), similar in nature to a vertebrate heel strike impacting the surface prior to the rest of the foot.
evidence: Analysis of spatiotemporal force patterns shown in Figure 6, with comparison to vertebrate locomotion.

claim: The posterior medial zone of the protopodia acts as a vaulting point functioning as a 'point d'appui' (point of support) as proposed in other soft-bodied animals.
source: We propose that this zone of the protopodia acts as a vaulting point for the protopodia, functioning as a 'point d'appui' (point of support) as proposed in other soft-bodied animals (Trueman, 1975; Valentine, 1989).
evidence: Inference based on force measurements (Figure 6) and citations to theoretical frameworks for soft-bodied locomotion.

claim: The contraction of musculature responsible for sequestration acts to move haemolymph into the protopodia, thus exerting increased pressure onto the substrate while contact area decreases.
source: We propose that the contraction of the musculature responsible for sequestration acts to move haemolymph into the protopodia, thus exerting an increased pressure onto the substrate while the contact area decreases as a consequence of the initiation of sequestration.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on observed force patterns during swing initiation (Figure 5).

claim: The outer region of protopodia deploys transiently to provide greater friction for subsequent segments, allowing the contractile wave to progress unimpeded by resultant reaction forces.
source: This may reflect a transient anchoring mechanism – specifically, this anchor region deploys to provide greater friction for the subsequent segments (Figure 7c). This would allow the contractile wave to progress unimpeded by resultant reaction forces.
evidence: Inference based on observed temporal patterns of contact area expansion and retraction (Figure 6).

claim: Drosophila larvae are proficient at crawling over wet surfaces where mucoid adhesion is reduced or impossible.
source: However, Drosophila larvae are proficient at crawling over wet surfaces where mucoid adhesion is reduced or impossible (Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).
evidence: Behavioral observation supported by citation to literature.

claim: Larvae can adhere to dry surfaces but have difficulty moving over these, although mucoid adhesion would provide optimal anchorage in this context.
source: Larvae can adhere to dry surfaces but have difficulty moving over these, although mucoid adhesion would provide optimal anchorage in this context.
evidence: Behavioral observation based on established knowledge of larval locomotion.

claim: Water surface films appear to facilitate larval locomotion in general, but the biomechanical mechanisms by which this occurs remain unclear.
source: Water surface films appear to facilitate larval locomotion in general, but the biomechanical mechanisms by which this occurs remain unclear.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap based on observations.

claim: Protopodia act to provide an optimal balance between anchorage and adhesion depending on the environmental context.
source: We propose that protopodia act to provide an optimal balance between anchorage and adhesion depending on the environmental context.
evidence: Proposed functional interpretation based on observed force patterns and behavioral context.

claim: Drosophila larvae use a sophisticated process of articulating, positioning, and sequestering protopodia to enable movement over terrain.
source: Overall, our work suggests that Drosophila larvae use a sophisticated process of articulating, positioning, and sequestering protopodia to enable movement over terrain.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all kinematic and force measurement data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Locomotion is a fundamental behaviour in the Animal Kingdom.
source: Locomotion is a fundamental behaviour in the Animal Kingdom.
evidence: General statement based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Action against a substrate or fluid produces forces, thereby translating the body in space, which is a unifying characteristic of diverse locomotion strategies.
source: Key to these different strategies is one unifying characteristic: action against a substrate or fluid produces forces, thereby translating the body in space.
evidence: Fundamental principle of locomotion based on physics and established biological knowledge.

claim: In aquatic environments, forces acting within fluids can be visualised via the waves of distortion they cause, facilitating the development of detailed theories of movement.
source: In an aquatic environment, forces acting within fluids can be visualised via the waves of distortion they cause, thus facilitating the development of detailed theories of movement (Gray and LIissmann, 1964).
evidence: Statement about aquatic locomotion supported by citation to classic literature.

claim: In terrestrial settings, substrates are often rigid and therefore prevent direct visualisation of ground reaction forces generated by animals.
source: In terrestrial settings, however, substrates are often rigid and therefore prevent direct visualisation of the ground reaction forces (GRFs) generated by animals.
evidence: Statement of technical challenge in studying terrestrial locomotion based on established knowledge.

claim: Interactions with substrates have been extensively studied in animals with articulating skeletons due to the ability to calculate output forces from lever physics combined with measurements of joint angles.
source: Interactions with substrates have been extensively studied in animals with articulating skeletons (i.e. rigid-bodied animals) due to the ability to calculate output forces from lever physics combined with measurements of joint angles (Audu et al., 2007; Bobbert et al., 2007).
evidence: Summary of existing research approaches supported by citations to literature.

claim: Much less is known about substrate interactions and ground reaction forces in soft-bodied animals without rigid internal or external skeletons.
source: However, much less is known about substrate interactions and GRFs in soft-bodied animals without rigid internal or external skeletons.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap based on literature review.

claim: Soft-bodied animals must anchor a part of their body when another part is in motion to prevent net progression being impeded by an equal but opposite reaction force, consistent with Newton's third law of motion.
source: However, they too must anchor a part of their body when another part is in motion to prevent net progression being impeded by an equal but opposite reaction force, that is, their movements must obey Newton's third law of motion (Trueman, 1975).
evidence: Fundamental physics principle applied to soft-bodied locomotion, supported by citation.

claim: Soft bodies pose a difficult control problem owing to their highly nonlinear physical properties and virtually unlimited degrees of freedom.
source: Furthermore, soft bodies pose a difficult control problem owing to their highly nonlinear physical properties and virtually unlimited degrees of freedom.
evidence: Statement of biomechanical challenge based on established understanding of soft materials.

claim: Dynamic anchoring has long been postulated to be at the heart of soft-bodied locomotion.
source: Dynamic anchoring has long since been postulated to be at the heart of soft-bodied locomotion (Tanaka et al., 2012), but understanding the mechanisms by which soft animals achieve this remains an open problem.
evidence: Statement of theoretical framework and knowledge gap supported by citation.

claim: Prior work on caterpillars, leeches, and Caenorhabditis elegans provided key insights and foundational observations for the inspiration of soft robot design.
source: Prior work on caterpillars (van Griethuijsen and Trimmer, 2014; Lin and Trimmer, 2010; Lin and Trimmer, 2012; Lin et al., 2011), leeches (Cacciatore et al., 2000; Kampowski et al., 2016) and Caenorhabditis elegans (Fang-Yen et al., 2010; Gjorgjieva et al., 2014) provided key insights and have provided foundational observations for the inspiration of soft robot design
evidence: Summary of prior research supported by multiple citations.

claim: A lack of methods with sufficient spatiotemporal resolution for measuring ground reaction forces in freely behaving animals has limited progress in understanding soft-bodied locomotion.
source: however, a lack of methods with sufficient spatiotemporal resolution for measuring GRFs in freely behaving animals has limited progress.
evidence: Statement of technical limitation based on literature review.

claim: In the field of cellular mechanobiology, many new force measuring techniques have been developed which allow measurement of comparatively small forces from soft structures exhibiting low inertia.
source: However, in the field of cellular mechanobiology, many new force measuring techniques have been developed which allow measurement of comparatively small forces from soft structures exhibiting low inertia (Krieg et al., 2019; Mohammed et al., 2019; Zancla et al., 2022) often with relatively high spatial resolution.
evidence: Summary of technical developments in cellular mechanobiology supported by citations.

claim: Atomic force microscopy is problematic for studying animal behaviour due to the risk of the laser and probe influencing behaviour.
source: This approach is problematic for studying animal behaviour due to the risk of the laser and probe influencing behaviour.
evidence: Statement of technical limitation based on understanding of AFM methodology.

claim: Traction force microscopy allows for probe-free measurement of forces but has insufficient temporal resolution for measuring forces produced by many behaving animals.
source: This technique allows for probe-free measurement of forces, but has insufficient temporal resolution for the measurement of forces produced by many behaving animals, despite recent improvements (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement of technical limitation supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: Micropillar arrays provide excellent temporal resolution but with limited spatial resolution for measuring horizontally aligned traction forces.
source: This approach provides excellent temporal resolution but with limited spatial resolution (Schoen et al., 2010; Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement of technical characteristics supported by citations to literature.

claim: ERISM allows reference-free mapping of substrate interactions and calculation of vertically directed ground reaction forces used in cell migration.
source: This technique allows reference-free mapping of substrate interactions as well as calculation of vertically directed GRFs used in cell migration (Kronenberg et al., 2017b; Liehm et al., 2018; Dalaka et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of ERISM capabilities supported by citations to prior publications.

claim: Great strides have been made in understanding the neural and genetic underpinnings of locomotion in the Drosophila larva.
source: In parallel, great strides have been made in understanding the neural and genetic underpinnings of locomotion in the Drosophila larva (Fushiki et al., 2016; Zwart et al., 2016; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016; Pulver et al., 2015; Heckscher et al., 2012), a genetically tractable soft-bodied model organism (Brand and Perrimon, 1993).
evidence: Summary of research progress supported by multiple citations.

claim: Data on biomechanical forces generated during substrate interactions in Drosophila larvae remain extremely limited.
source: While computational modelling and biomechanical measurements have provided an initial knowledgebase (Loveless et al., 2019; Loveless et al., 2021; Gjorgjieva et al., 2013), data on biomechanical forces generated during substrate interactions in Drosophila larvae remain extremely limited (Khare et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: Development of methods for measuring ground reaction forces in Drosophila larvae would enable fully integrated neurogenetic-biomechanical approaches to understanding soft-bodied movement.
source: Development of methods for measuring GRFs in this model organism would enable fully integrated neurogenetic-biomechanical approaches to understanding soft-bodied movement and fulfil calls from the modelling community for more biomechanics data (Tytell et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement of research need supported by citation to modeling community perspective.

claim: Ordinary larval behaviour is maintained on collagen-treated microcavity substrates.
source: First, we confirmed that ordinary larval behaviour is maintained on collagen-treated microcavity substrates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Behavioral validation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total number of behaviors per second is not significantly different between agarose substrates and elastic cavities with collagen coating.
source: Total number of behaviours per second is not significantly different between agarose substrates and elastic cavities with collagen coating according to a two-sample t-test (t(18) = -1.24, p=0.23).
evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral frequencies shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Distance travelled as percentage of body length is not significantly different between agarose substrates and microcavities.
source: Distance travelled as % of body length was not significantly different between the two substrates according to a two-sample t-test (t(18) = 1.34, p=0.20).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mean duration of forward waves is not significantly different on microcavities compared to agarose.
source: The mean duration of five forward waves was not significantly different on microcavities compared to agarose according to a two-sample t-test (t(18) = 0.62, p=0.54).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: WARP is largely limited to measurements of forces in the vertical direction.
source: However, WARP microscopy is largely limited to measurements of forces in the vertical direction, and though we can make inferences such as this as they are a consequence of fundamental laws of physics, we present this conclusion as a testable prediction which could be confirmed using a force measurement technique more tuned to horizontally directed forces relative to the substrate.
evidence: Statement of technical limitation based on the physics of the measurement technique.

claim: The effective frame rate of resultant displacement and stress maps is equal to half of the recorded frame rate of the interference maps in WARP.
source: Further, as a result of the combining of the two wavelengths, the effective frame rate of the resultant displacement and stress maps is equal to half of the recorded frame rate of the interference maps.
evidence: Technical description of WARP methodology.

claim: Using WARP in conjunction with high-speed traction force microscopy could provide a fully integrated picture of underlying vertical and horizontal traction forces during larval locomotion.
source: Using WARP in conjunction with high-speed TFM (possibly using tuneable elastomers presented here) could provide a fully integrated picture of underlying vertical and horizontal traction forces during larval locomotion.
evidence: Proposed future experimental approach based on complementary capabilities of different techniques.

claim: The FEM simulation estimated a total applied force of 114.8 nN compared to an actual applied force of 111 nN, representing a relative difference of only 3.4%.
source: Comparing this simulated force to the applied force of 111 nN, we found the relative difference to be only 3.4%, with our simulation estimating a total applied force of 114.8 nN.
evidence: Validation experiment using AFM shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The vertical GRFs produced by individual protopodia are roughly three orders of magnitude less than the 17 mN recorded from an entire 1.72 g Manduca sexta caterpillar.
source: The measured vertical GRFs produced by the individual protopodia of each segment were in the 1–7 µN range, roughly three orders of magnitude less than the 17 mN recorded from an entire 1.72 g M. sexta caterpillar (Lin and Trimmer, 2010).
evidence: Comparative analysis of force measurements with citation to literature on caterpillar forces.

claim: Surface tension produced by a water droplet likely serves a role in adhering the animal to the substrate.
source: This surface tension produced by such a water droplet likely serves a role in adhering the animal to the substrate.
evidence: Inference based on observed upward forces in WARP imaging (Figure 4a).

claim: During forward waves, protopodia detach completely during swing period, suggesting surface tension-related adhesion force can be easily overcome by the behaving animal.
source: However, during forward waves, we found that protopodia detached completely during SwP, suggesting this surface tension-related adhesion force can be easily overcome by the behaving animal.
evidence: Direct observation from WARP imaging shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Larvae horizontally slide posterior regions forward before invaginating and sequestering denticles, which explains how they prevent rough denticulated cuticle from creating drag due to friction against the direction of the wave.
source: This observation, coupled with our lateral imaging of protopodia in constrained animals, explains how larvae prevent their rough denticulated cuticle from creating drag due to friction against the direction of the wave.
evidence: Inference based on combined observations from lateral imaging (Figure 1c) and WARP imaging (Figure 4a).

claim: Canton S wildtype larvae were used for all experiments.
source: Canton S (CS) wildtype larvae were used for all experiments (Fly Base Identifier: FBsn0000274).
evidence: Experimental methods description.

claim: Animals were raised on standard cornmeal and yeast medium at 25°C with a 12 hr light-dark cycle.
source: Animals were raised on standard cornmeal and yeast medium (17.4 g/L yeast, 73.1 g/L cornmeal, 5.8 g/L agar, 4.8 ml/L propionate) at 25°C with a 12 hr light-dark cycle except where explicitly stated otherwise.
evidence: Experimental methods description.

claim: Microcavities consisted of two semi-transparent, flexible gold mirrors sandwiching a transparent polymer rubber made from a mixture of siloxanes with discrete Young's moduli.
source: These microcavities consisted of two semi-transparent, flexible gold mirrors sandwiching a transparent polymer rubber that was made from a mixture of siloxanes with discrete Young's moduli to adjust the resulting stiffness (Palchesko et al., 2012).
evidence: Technical description of microcavity fabrication with citation to methodology.

claim: Force-distance curves were fitted to a height-corrected Hertz model to determine the Young's modulus of each cavity.
source: The microcavities were characterised using AFM and the resulting force distance curves (Figure 3b) were fitted to a height-corrected Hertz model to determine the Young's modulus of each cavity (Dimitriadis et al., 2002).
evidence: Description of characterization methodology with citation.

claim: All WARP videos were recorded at 120 FPS, producing displacement maps with an effective frame rate of 60 FPS.
source: All WARP videos were recorded at 120 FPS, producing displacement maps with an effective frame rate of 60 FPS, using a ×4 magnification objective.
evidence: Technical specification of imaging parameters.
